To estimate the causal effect of rural income growth on Hindu-Muslim riots, I will use an instrumental variables (two-stage least squares) strategy. I will instrument for the endogenous treatment, annual district rural income growth per person, using `works_draw` (which equals 1 if the district was randomly selected in 1985 for the central government's rural public-works wage program, and 0 otherwise, interacted with post-1985 indicators as appropriate). This instrument is relevant—raising rural income growth by 1.2 percentage points on average—and satisfies independence and the exclusion restriction because districts were chosen by random draw and the program changed nothing else in drawn districts. In contrast, `monsoon_dev` is unsuitable as an instrument because the exclusion restriction is violated: rainfall deviations increase riots in dam-fed districts where crop income is unaffected, indicating a direct non-income effect of rainfall on riots. For precision and balance checks, I will include state and year fixed effects alongside baseline 1981 district covariates (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`) and cluster standard errors at the district level. The main threat to this design is whether the new roads and ponds constructed under the public-works program directly affected riot incidence or reporting (for example, by altering mobility or water access) independently of rural income growth.

CANDIDATES:
works_draw | plausible
monsoon_dev | violated
INSTRUMENT: works_draw

To estimate the causal effect of district rural income growth on the number of Hindu-Muslim riots, I will use an instrumental variables (2SLS) design. I will instrument for annual rural income growth using `works_draw` (interacted with a post-1985 indicator in a panel specification with district and year fixed effects, or in post-1985 cross-sections controlling for 1981 baseline characteristics `pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`). The instrument is relevant and exogenous because the 1985 central government lottery randomly assigned 145 districts to a wage-paying public-works program, raising their rural income growth by 1.2 percentage points on average while changing nothing else. I reject `monsoon_dev` as an alternative instrument because it violates the exclusion restriction: districts downstream of irrigation dams experience more riots during below-average monsoons even though canal water keeps their crop income unchanged, showing that rainfall affects riots through non-income channels. The main threat to the `works_draw` design is potential spillover effects, such as migration or wage adjustments in neighboring non-drawn districts, or subtle direct effects of the newly built roads and ponds on riot logistics. Standard errors will be clustered at the district level to account for serial correlation across years.

CANDIDATES:

monsoon_dev | violated
INSTRUMENT: works_draw

I will estimate the causal effect of annual district rural income growth per person on the number of Hindu-Muslim riots using an instrumental variables (2SLS) design. For the post-1985 period (or interacting the lottery indicator with a post-1985 indicator in the full 1982–1995 panel with district and year fixed effects), I will instrument rural income growth with `works_draw`, the 1985 random assignment of districts to the central government's rural public-works program. Randomization ensures independence, the 1.2 percentage point average boost to rural income growth provides a strong first stage, and the codebook confirms the program changed nothing else in drawn districts. In contrast, I reject `monsoon_dev` as an instrument because the documentation notes that dam-irrigated districts whose crop income is insulated from monsoon fluctuations still experience comparable increases in riots during deficit monsoon years, violating the exclusion restriction. I will include baseline 1981 district covariates (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`) and `state` fixed effects to improve precision and cluster standard errors at the district level. The main threat to identification is that road and pond construction or program wage employment might directly affect intergroup contact, mobility, or time allocation in ways that influence riots independently of rural income growth.

I will estimate the causal effect of district rural income growth on the number of Hindu-Muslim riots using an instrumental variables (2SLS) design. As my primary instrument for annual rural income growth, I will use `works_draw`, which indicates whether a district was randomly selected in 1985 for a central government rural public-works wage program. Because the 1985 draw was random, raises rural income growth by 1.2 percentage points on average, and explicitly changed nothing else in the drawn districts, it satisfies relevance, independence, and the exclusion restriction. I will control for baseline 1981 district characteristics (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, `riots_prev`), state fixed effects (`state`), and year fixed effects to improve precision. I also considered `monsoon_dev` (monsoon rainfall deviation) as a panel instrument with district and year fixed effects, which is a plausible alternative, though rainfall shocks can sometimes directly affect riot logistics or heat-related aggression independently of income. The main threat to the `works_draw` strategy is that the cross-sectional lottery occurred in 1985 while the sample begins in 1982, requiring that we either interact the lottery indicator with a post-1985 indicator or restrict the IV estimation to the post-1985 period when the program was active.

I will estimate the causal effect of annual rural income per person growth on the number of Hindu-Muslim riots using an instrumental variables (two-stage least squares) strategy. The primary instrument is `works_draw`, an indicator for whether a district was randomly selected in 1985 for the central government's rural public-works wage program, which increases rural income growth by 1.2 percentage points on average and is randomized across districts. To improve precision and account for baseline differences across the 290 districts, the specification will include state and year fixed effects along with pre-treatment 1981 census and riot controls (`pop_1981`, `muslim_share`, `urban_share`, `literacy`, and `riots_prev`), with standard errors clustered at the district level. I also considered `monsoon_dev` (monsoon rainfall deviation) as an alternative instrument within a district and year fixed-effects panel, but it is doubtful because rainfall can directly affect riot logistics, agricultural prices, or migration outside the rural income channel. The main threat to identification with `works_draw` is a potential violation of the exclusion restriction if the newly constructed roads and ponds—or workers congregating at public-works sites—directly altered inter-group contact or police mobility, though the program documentation indicates the intervention changed nothing else in drawn districts.

I will estimate the causal effect of county voter turnout on the incumbent party's presidential vote share using an instrumental variables (two-stage least squares) strategy. The endogenous treatment is county turnout (in percentage points of the voting-age population), the outcome is the incumbent party's county vote share, and the instrument is `reminder_draw`, an indicator for whether the county was randomly selected to receive a nonpartisan mailed election reminder. Because `reminder_draw` is randomly assigned, increases turnout by 2.4 percentage points on average, and conveys no partisan information, it satisfies both relevance and the exclusion restriction. In contrast, I will not use election-day rainfall (`eday_rain`) as an instrument because post-election surveys show that rain directly alters voters' risk preferences and makes those who still vote more likely to support the incumbent party, violating the exclusion restriction. The specification will include county and election-year fixed effects, along with baseline county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`) to improve precision and cluster standard errors at the county level. The main threat to this design is that the local average treatment effect (LATE) for voters induced to turn out by a mailed reminder may differ from the effect of turnout changes driven by other forces, or that the reminder inadvertently mobilized incumbent-leaning voters more through differential salience rather than pure turnout.

CANDIDATES:
reminder_draw | plausible
eday_rain | violated
INSTRUMENT: reminder_draw

I propose an instrumental variables (2SLS) design using `reminder_draw` as an instrument for county voter turnout to estimate its causal effect on the incumbent president's party vote share. The `reminder_draw` indicator satisfies relevance—raising county turnout by 2.4 percentage points on average—and exogeneity, as it comes from a random draw of a nonpartisan reminder that changed nothing else in drawn counties. We will include county and election-year fixed effects alongside baseline county covariates (`dem_prev`, `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, `median_inc`) to improve precision and cluster standard errors at the county level. We will also consider `eday_rain` (election-day rainfall deviations) as an alternative instrument, though it is less clean than the randomized draw because weather could directly affect incumbent support through voter mood or differential partisan composition of marginal voters. The main threat to our primary specification is potential interference (spillovers) across county borders or if the reminder subtly altered voter composition or information in ways that directly affected party preference independently of the aggregate turnout rate.

CANDIDATES:
reminder_draw | plausible
eday_rain | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: reminder_draw

The main threat to this design is a potential violation of the exclusion restriction or monotonicity if the nonpartisan reminder subtly alters the salience of incumbent performance among always-takers or induces differential compositional shifts beyond the local average treatment effect of compliers.

To estimate the causal effect of racial residential segregation on city direct general expenditure per resident, I propose an instrumental variables (two-stage least squares) strategy using the 2000 and 2010 post-draw census waves (or a panel interacting the lottery with post-1990 indicators). I will instrument for the city's multigroup entropy segregation index using `audit_grant`, an indicator for whether the city was randomly selected in the 1990 federal lottery to receive a fair-housing testing grant. Because the grant was assigned by a random draw, paid directly to a nonprofit rather than the municipal government, and reduced the segregation index by 2.2 points in later census years while changing nothing else in drawn cities, it satisfies relevance, independence, and the exclusion restriction. The specification will include state-by-year fixed effects and baseline or pre-treatment city covariates (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, `own_rate`, and `region`) to improve precision, with standard errors clustered at the city level. I reject `waterways` as an instrument because every boundary stream in the 1920 survey became a municipal or school-district boundary, meaning `waterways` directly alters jurisdictional fragmentation and local public spending outside of within-city racial segregation. The main threat to the `audit_grant` design is potential weak-instrument bias or spillovers if fair-housing audits directly influenced residents' political mobilization or local housing markets in ways that affected per-capita municipal spending independently of residential segregation.

CANDIDATES:
audit_grant | plausible
waterways | violated
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

To estimate the causal effect of racial residential segregation on city direct general expenditure per resident, I will use an instrumental variables (2SLS) design. I will instrument for the multigroup entropy segregation index in later census years (2000 and 2010) using `audit_grant`, an indicator for whether the city was randomly selected in the 1990 federal lottery to receive a fair-housing testing grant. This instrument is relevant and exogenous because random assignment lowered the segregation index by 2.2 points on average in subsequent decades, and the grant went to a nonprofit rather than the city government, changing nothing else in drawn cities. The specification will include state-by-year fixed effects and baseline city controls (`log_pop`, `pct_black`, `pct_hisp`, `med_income`, `own_rate`), restricting the sample to cities eligible for the 1990 draw. By contrast, I reject `waterways` as an instrument because the documentation notes that 1920 boundary streams directly determined the number of separately governed municipalities and school districts, violating the exclusion restriction by directly affecting local public spending fragmentation. The main threat to the `audit_grant` design is potential weak-instrument bias or finite-sample imbalance if the lottery must be conditioned on unobserved eligibility strata, which I will diagnose using first-stage F-statistics and pre-treatment balance checks on 1980 and 1990 outcomes.

CANDIDATES:

waterways | violated
INSTRUMENT: audit_grant

I reject `waterways` as an instrument because streams served as municipal and school district boundaries, meaning cities with more waterways are in more fragmented metropolitan areas, which directly alters local government responsibilities and spending per resident. The main threat to the `audit_grant` design is a potential exclusion restriction violation if fair-housing audits indirectly influenced municipal spending through channels other than residential integration, such as heightened local political activism or changes in the housing market and property tax base.
